fields.body: قصر خزام ہفوف کے مغرب میں محلہ المزروعیہ کے کنارے واقع ہے۔ یہ قلعہ 1220 ہجری (1805 عیسوی) میں امام سعود بن عبد العزیز نے تعمیر کیا، جو پہلی سعودی ریاست کے تیسرے امام تھے۔ یہ ان قلعوں کے سلسلے کی ایک کڑی تھا جو الاحساء کی حفاظت اور اس کے مغربی راستوں کی نگرانی کے لیے بنائے گئے تھے۔ اس کا نام “زمام” سے نکلا ہے، یعنی وہ مہار جس سے اونٹوں کو لے کر چلتے ہیں؛ یہ نام اس علاقے پر قلعے کی گرفت کی علامت ہے۔ اس کی مستطیل فصیل ایک طرف تقریباً 70 میٹر اور دوسری طرف تقریباً 80 میٹر لمبی ہے، اور چھ برج اس کی حفاظت کرتے ہیں، جن میں سے زیادہ تر مخروطی شکل کے ہیں۔ فصیل کے اندر کھلا صحن، مسجد، بیٹھک، کنواں اور اصطبل ہیں۔ بعد میں یہ قلعہ قبائل کے معاملات سنبھالنے اور پانی کے ذرائع پر ہونے والے جھگڑے نمٹانے کا مرکز بنا۔ 2017 میں اس کی مرمت ہوئی اور اسے سیاحوں کے لیے کھول دیا گیا۔ آج یہ “الاحساء کا نخلستان” کے بارہ حصوں میں سے ایک ہے۔ یہ نخلستان 2018 میں یونیسکو کی فہرست میں درج ہوا۔

fields.body: بیت البیعہ (یعنی بیعت کا گھر) ہفوف کے وسط میں، محلہ الکوت میں ہے، اور بیت الملا کے نام سے بھی معروف ہے۔ یہاں سے چند قدم کے فاصلے پر سوق القیصریہ نامی بازار اور قصر ابراہیم ہیں۔ یہ گھر 1203 ہجری (1788 عیسوی) میں الاحساء کے قاضی شیخ عبد الرحمن بن عمر بن محمد الملا نے تعمیر کیا۔ اس کا رقبہ 705 مربع میٹر ہے۔ بعد میں یہ عبد اللطیف بن عبد الرحمن الملا (1853–1921) کا گھر رہا، جو الملا خاندان کے بزرگ، فقیہ اور قاضی تھے۔ شاہ عبد العزیز 28 جمادی الاول 1331 ہجری (4 مئی 1913 عیسوی) کو الاحساء پہنچے تو سب سے پہلے اسی گھر میں داخل ہوئے۔ یہیں الاحساء کے لوگوں نے ان کے ہاتھ پر بیعت کی اور سعودی ریاست میں شامل ہو گئے۔ یوں یہ گھر جدید سعودی ریاست میں الاحساء کی شمولیت کی علامت بن گیا، اور یہ الاحساء کے نمایاں ترین تاریخی اور سیاسی مقامات میں سے ایک ہے۔ آثار قدیمہ اور عجائب گھروں کے سعودی ادارے نے 2005 سے 2007 تک اس کی مرمت کی۔ تب سے الاحساء کے لوگ سعودی قومی دن یہیں مناتے آئے ہیں۔ اب یہ ایک عجائب گھر ہے: اس کے کمروں میں نوادرات، اوزار، مخطوطات اور تصویریں رکھی ہیں، جو اس گھر کی کہانی سناتی ہیں۔ لکڑی کی کھڑکیوں والا یہ سفید گھر دو منزلہ ہے۔ نچلی منزل پر مہمانوں کے استقبال کا ایک بڑا صحن ہے جس کی طرف اندرونی جھروکے کھلتے ہیں؛ یہیں مہمانوں کے بیٹھنے کی جگہیں ہیں، اور یہیں لباس اور ذاتی استعمال کی چیزیں نمائش کے لیے رکھی ہیں۔ اوپر کی منزل کے کمرے زیادہ تر سونے اور رہنے سہنے کے لیے تھے، اور ان کی دیواروں پر تاریخی اور وضاحتی تصویریں لگی ہیں۔

Five points off: «ایک دوسرے کو کاٹتی محراب دار چھتیں» was read twice and not pictured, and «بیلن نما» made him smile — both kept for want of a wording that says as much; «منصوبے کے تحت» is office language the source obliges; and five edits in two leaves are unread, the row among them in b1's wording, which no reader has seen either.

compliance.why: «مسجد الجبری» feminine throughout («بنی ہے», «رہی», «کھلی ہے»); «بنو جبر» in summary and body; «سیف بن زامل الجبری» with its article; «تقریباً 1,600» grouped as the English groups it; the visiting row equal to jawatha-mosque's byte for byte, an inner «؛» and no final stop; the programme unmarked because the source only describes it. Two points off: «بنو جبر» and the programme are pending; the row, the dropped «زندہ» and the «درس و تدریس» compound are forms of this round, unproofed.

fit.why: For a Muslim family this is the page of the five that sits closest to home, and «زائرین» fits a mosque. Two points off: the label «زیارت» suggests to this reader 'something more than a mosque' (ruled for every mosque page on a reader who found it to fit; his remark is on record); the request to dress modestly reads to him as written for someone who has never entered a mosque. That the page talks of a fee twice and says nothing of when to come or of women is the source's.

structure.why: Eleven leaves in pack order; three card rows by their ids; the label «زیارت» without stop or bracket; the area line leads with the larger place as a bare name (ruling P20); no hours row is invented where the source has none.

fields.title: مسجد الجبری
fields.summary: محلہ الکوت میں بنو جبر کے دور کی ایک مسجد، جسے پندرہویں صدی عیسوی سے نمازیوں نے آباد رکھا ہے۔
fields.body: مسجد الجبری محلہ الکوت میں قصر ابراہیم کے قریب واقع ہے؛ الکوت پرانے ہفوف کا قدیم ترین محلہ ہے۔ یہ مسجد الاحساء کی قدیم ترین اور مشہور ترین مساجد میں سے ایک ہے۔ اسے سیف بن زامل الجبری نے بنو جبر کی ریاست کے دور میں، تقریباً 850 ہجری (1446 عیسوی) میں تعمیر کیا اور اس کے لیے کھیت اور کھجور کے باغ وقف کیے۔ یہ عبادت کے ساتھ ساتھ درس و تدریس اور علم کا مرکز بھی رہی۔ یہ مٹی اور چونے کے پتھر سے بنی ہے۔ ایک دوسرے کو کاٹتی محراب دار چھتیں، کئی برآمدے اور مختلف وضع کے گنبد اس کی پہچان ہیں، اور اس کا مینار بیلن نما ہے۔ اس میں تقریباً 1,600 نمازیوں کی گنجائش ہے۔ صدیوں کے دوران اس کی بار بار مرمت ہوئی؛ آخری مرمت 1437 ہجری (2016 عیسوی) میں تاریخی مساجد کی دیکھ بھال کے منصوبے کے تحت ہوئی، اور اس میں اصل تعمیراتی مواد برتا گیا۔ یہ آج بھی ایک آباد مسجد ہے۔

practical.label: داخلہ
practical.value: آباد مسجد، داخلے کی کوئی فیس نہیں

practical.label: زیارت
practical.value: زائرین کے لیے کھلی ہے؛ ساتر لباس پہن کر آئیں اور اس مقام کی حرمت کا خیال رکھیں

blind_reader_rulings.reason: The notice is the template's sentence (det.hoursNotice with det.hoursNotice.op, ruled in b0-ui under P27) and the reader calls it 'plain, natural Urdu'. What he could not do with it is the source's and the template's: none of the five pages has an operator link (pack: operatorUrl false on all five), so «اس مقام کی انتظامیہ» is not even a link here and no channel is named (SD14 of the calibration); and the template shows the notice wherever a card has rows it takes for hours or fees — on uqair-castle, whose hours row holds a status, and on jabri-mosque, which has no hours row and whose fee rows say that nothing is charged. Not a plain-text artifact on these pages. Recorded for the interface batch.

Not a leaf of this batch: «یہ مقام محفوظ کریں» and «محفوظ ہو گیا ✓» are the interface strings fav.add and fav.added, final in b0-ui and so pairs of the translation memory. Not ruled away: b1's reader read the button first as an appeal to protect the site too (b1 observation 1) — two readers, independently, on heritage pages; this one adds that the confirmation does not say where the place was saved. Recorded for the interface batch's next round. His 'nothing to report' on the share button, the copied-link message, the distance button, the maps link, the report link and the three location replies is recorded with it.

Both lines are interface strings of b0-ui (det.nearby.h, det.nearby.d), final there. The evidence is carried to that batch: «سیر مکمل کرنا» has now been heard as translated by three readers (b0-ui round 2, b1's, this one), and this reader wrote the remedy b1's reader wrote, almost word for word («… جو آپ اسی سیر میں دیکھ سکتے ہیں»). New from him: the heading «اپنا دن بھرپور بنائیں» is 'the one advertisement-voice line on otherwise sober pages'.

The interface string det.nearby.note (b0-ui), final there. Carried to that batch with b1's same remark: the qualifier trails after the verb. This reader names it as a pattern — 'the same tail-after-the-verb order I met again in two card rows' (observations 18 and 52): the visiting row is reordered in this round, as b1's judge ruled it; the status row of khuzam is the owner's confirmed statement and keeps the source's order, with his order on record. His wording for the note is recorded: «یہ فاصلے سیدھی لکیر میں ناپے گئے اندازے ہیں۔».

The accessible name of each photo is built by the template in every language: the title, a dash, det.photo and a number (pack, render order: 'alt = title + — + det.photo + n'). The attraction files carry no description of what a picture shows, and none may be invented. Not an artifact of the plain-text page: this is what a listener hears. Logged for the owner and recorded for the interface batch. The names inside these labels change with the titles («قصر محیرس», «قصر خزام»).

Applied where the word is this batch's own and the page is not a mosque: on khuzam the visitors of the fort are now «سیاح», the word of the card heading and of the dictionary's own example for a fort (item N29 of this file, the question b1's judge left to this batch). On the mosque page «زائرین» stays in the fixed row: b1's item N17, on a reader who said of the same word on a mosque 'the second fits'. The heading «سیاحوں کے لیے معلومات» above a mosque card is the interface's (det.visitInfo, b0-ui): b1's reader made the same remark, and it is recorded for that batch's next round.

Item N14, ruled in b1 round 1 for both attraction batches on this very observation and on b1's own: the titles are «قصر محیرس» and «قصر خزام», the places' own names, and the labelled brackets are gone. 'One word for the thing in title and text' is answered as far as a name allows: the name keeps the Arabic generic, which Urdu dictionaries gloss as a palace; the common noun is «قلعہ» in the summary and in the first lines of each body, never next to the name. The cost b1's judge stated stands and is his question to the next reader: a reader for whom «قصر» is a palace still meets «قلعہ» in the next line with nothing between.

Ruling P17, not reopened: no vowel marks and no pronunciation gloss are added to a name, and the build guard of ruling P8 rejects the kasra. The bracket that 'gave the same bare letters again' is gone with item N14. Recorded, not ruled away: b0-ui's open item N7 (three readers asked for vowel signs on a quoted Arabic word) now has a fourth reader asking for them on three names of forts; whoever may reopen P17 finds both there. That he could not say «محیرس» to a driver is charged under fit.

Neither source says what Al-Mubarraz is (a city; SD10 of the calibration made the same remark of Hofuf), and b1's entry for the name keeps the word 'city' out because the English does not have it. 'On the edge of' stands in the summary and 'north of' in the body and the area line, in BOTH languages (pack, reviewed divergences), and 'north of' is as open in the sources as in the Urdu. His first reading of «کے کنارے» as a bank or shore follows from not being told that the name is a town; nothing is added to tell him.

Applied for both faults that are the Urdu's: the colon with a verbless phrase after it, and — with observation 61 — the verb. The first sentence is his own; the apposition becomes a sentence of its own with a verb. NOT applied: dropping the apposition because the summary has said it — the body is a field read on its own, and item N14 wants the common noun in its opening. That 'watch' returns a third time further down is the source's ('watch-and-guard fort', 'a lookout post').

Both sources give the builder as 'Saud bin Abdulaziz (later Imam)' on muhairis and 'Imam Saud bin Abdulaziz, third imam of the First Saudi State' on khuzam (pack: 'one person, two title treatments'), and neither page says that 'Imam' is here the ruler's title. The Urdu says what each page says, with the Urdu word «امام»; a word such as 'of the state' on muhairis would import a fact of another page. Harm: a reader who opens only muhairis takes the builder for a man who later became a prayer leader.

No page says who is who: Saud bin Abdulaziz of the First Saudi State (1208 and 1220 AH) and King Abdulaziz (1913) stand on three pages with nothing to tell a reader that more than a century lies between two rulers of one house; the name of the earlier one is also that of a king of the 1950s. Nothing may be supplied: who King Abdulaziz was is in no source of these pages (stage 3 was tempted and held back). The names are written as their entries have them; the homonym is recorded in the entry.
His wording, whole: «ایک» before the adjective, and «ہے» for «بلند ہے», which he read as 'the tower is tall'.

CONFIRMED from the pack. The only hours on the page are, in both languages, those of 'the garden and walkway' («الحديقة والممشى يومياً»); the next row says 'Free entry' («مجاني») without saying to what; the body calls the green space 'a green park' («منتزه») where the card says 'garden' («الحديقة»); and nothing, in the summary, the body or the card, says whether the fort itself is entered — the body's last word on it is that it fell out of use. The Urdu names what the hours belong to before the hours, as both sources do, keeps the two source nouns as two words, and supplies nothing. What the reader made of it: 'I would drive the family there not knowing whether we will see a fort from inside or take an evening walk beside a wall.'

His wording («جب الاحساء میں میلے لگتے ہیں تو …»): «میلوں» is no longer there to be read as miles. That the sentence raises 'when?' is the source's: the festival seasons are neither named nor dated in either language.

Ruling P13 (4): 4 pm is a MEASURED point of the owner's ruling, «شام 4 بجے» on 20 pages against «سہ پہر 4 بجے» on 1, and b1's judge ruled on the same remark of its own reader that the table stands (item N10); a ruling is not reopened here. This is the second reader of the two attraction batches to say that in a timetable four o'clock is «سہ پہر»; both are on record with b1's one-line option for the owner, who made the ruling: «سہ پہر 4 بجے».

CONFIRMED from the pack: the body says 'Restored and opened to visitors in 2017' («رُمّم وافتُتح للزوار عام 2017م») and the only card row says 'Currently closed for restoration and heritage development' («مغلق حالياً …»); the two languages agree with each other, and the summary, which is the page's search description and index card, says nothing of a closure. The site owner confirmed on 2026-10-12 that the fort IS closed and that both statements stand as they are. The Urdu carries both, each at its source's strength, with no word between them: no 'but', no 'again', no 'for now', no date. What a reader made of it: 'The paragraph ends by telling me the fort was restored and opened; nothing in it says it is shut now. Had I stopped at the paragraph, I would have gone'; and the card left him unable to plan — closed until when, and can it at least be seen from outside? Neither is in the source.

A status is the site's own statement, and this one the owner confirmed on 2026-10-12: the row stands as the source has it and is not softened or dropped. Both sources lead with the status ('Currently closed for …', «مغلق حالياً لأعمال …»), and so does the Urdu, on purpose since stage 1: it is the only place on the page that tells a visitor not to come, and he found it there (his own serious observation 17 quotes it). His reordering puts the reason first and drops «فی الحال», the source's 'currently': a repair that changes how the site words a statement of its own goes to the owner (ruling P25), and no earlier line translated this row to follow. The other two points are the source's: 'heritage development' is all either language says of the work, and 'at present' is said twice by the source's own label and value ('Current status' over 'Currently closed', «الوضع الحالي» over «مغلق حالياً»). One-line option for the owner, his order with the adverb kept: «مرمت اور ورثے کی ترقی کے کاموں کی وجہ سے فی الحال بند ہے». That the reason trails after the verb is charged under nativeness.

Both sources say the name derives from 'zimam' and neither says how «خزام» comes out of «زمام» (the two share no first letter): logged since stage 1. The Urdu quotes the word the source quotes and gives the source's own explanation; the reader found the gloss with «مہار» 'exactly the right Urdu word'. Harm: one of the two words looks like a typing slip, and he went back to the title to check.

The template prints the number of the World Heritage component bare after the badge label, in every language (det.unesco + the component id). Logged by b0-ui (its readers took 1563 for a year, a range, a code) and by b1 (observation 6); nothing in the page fields explains it and nothing may be added. Recorded for the interface batch.

Item N16, ruled by b1's judge on this very observation together with its own reader's: no «اس مقام» before the quoted name, and the inscription in its own sentence so that 2018 belongs to the oasis. The summary has neither fault and stands. Not applied: «یونیسکو کے عالمی ورثے کی فہرست» — this page's sources say 'UNESCO-listed' and 'inscribed by UNESCO' and do not name the list (the badge does); his «یہ پورا مقام» is b1's «یہ نخلستان».

Item N24: «ضرب» is gone. His own remedy, the length-and-breadth form of the other page, is barred by the fence: on muhairis the two sides are equal ('twenty metres a side'), here neither source says which figure is the length. That one page gives its measure in words and the other in figures is the sources' own (both write 'twenty' in words and '70 by 80' in digits).

Second point applied in his words («مخروطی شکل کے»). First point not applied: that the towers 'guard' the wall is the image of both sources, and the register does not outrank the content of the field's source (ruling P24).

'On Hofuf's western edge' (summary), 'on the edge of Al-Mazrouiyah district in western Hofuf' (body) and 'west of Hofuf' (area) are the source's three ways of placing one fort (pack, reviewed divergences), and whether the district lies inside the town is not settled by the page in either language; the Urdu phrase is as open as the Arabic's «غربي الهفوف».

The name is built from its Arabic spelling (rulings P1 and P17: the article kept, the final letter as U+06C1), and no gloss stands in a title or a path line (P3c-labels, ruled in b0-ui). The gloss he asks for is where the ruling puts it, once, at the first mention in the body, and he says it 'clears it at once'. Recorded in the entry: in the title he first took «البیعہ» from the word for a sale.

His wording: «بھی». A repair of form under ruling P23, logged as a source defect; the approved Russian body says 'also known as' as well. Which of the two names a visitor should ask for is still not said by the page, in any language.

The family's name is written as the Arabic writes it, article kept (item N27, ruled in b1 round 1; b1's adopted «مسجد شیخ محمد بن ابی بکر الملا»), and the summary, which renders first, already says «الملا خاندان» — the word that tells a reader it is a family. A form without the article («ملا خاندان») would read as 'the mullah family' outright. Recorded in the entries: for a moment he could not tell a surname from a title.
His own two sentences.

The bracket is the source's: '(1853–1921)' in the English and «(1853–1921م)» in the Arabic, Gregorian only, with no word saying birth and death, on a page whose other dates lead with the Hijri year. Nothing is computed and no Hijri years are taken from the reference article that has them. Whether the Abdulrahman of this man's name is the judge who built the house in 1788 is not said by either source (the dates make it impossible, as he worked out). The form of the bracket is ruled (b1's item N13).

Item P3c, ruled in b1 round 1 with both candidate forms on record and applied here: the souq's bracket becomes «سوق القیصریہ نامی بازار»; the page keeps one «(یعنی …)» bracket, on its own name. The brackets that worked 'the other way round' on the two fort pages are gone with item N14. What Al-Qaisariyah is beyond a bazaar is not in this page's sources.

'The First Saudi State' (muhairis, khuzam), 'the Saudi state' and 'the modern Saudi state' (baiah, summary and body) are the sources' three labels, and no page says how they relate. The summary and the body of baiah say almost the same sentence because the sources do. One Urdu noun, «ریاست», carries all three.

The sentence is the site's own claim, word for word: 'one of its foremost historical and political landmarks' («ومن أهم معالمها التاريخية والسياسية»), a superlative that stands under 'one of' in both sources. A plainer wording would change how the site states it (ruling P25). The name is written a third time on purpose: 'its' can be Al-Ahsa's or the state's in both languages, and the Urdu pronoun would point at the state, which stands nearer.

Applied for the range, in his own form (b1's items N13 and N22). The body's name stays as it is and its entry stays pending: it is a descriptive rendering of a name the English itself blurs by adding 'Saudi', which the Arabic does not have; that he could not tell a name from a description is recorded in the entry. It takes no quotation marks: b1's sahood names a body the same way («ادارہ ورثہ نے …»), and item N16 marks the names of a property and of a programme, not of a body that acts.

Two points applied, each with the smallest change: the postposition of the balconies (change b-balcony: «جس کی طرف»), and one word between the two «اور». Third point not applied: whose clothing and personal effects are on show is not said by either source.

'Historical and explanatory photographs' / «صور تاريخية وإرشادية» is all the sources say; «وضاحتی تصویریں» renders the second adjective word for word. The Arabic adds that they tell the story of the house, which the English does not carry and the Urdu does not import.
One location, one word: «وسط» in the body as in the card, which is also the Arabic's one word for both.

The English body is one paragraph of four long sentences (1331 characters) where the Arabic has five paragraphs, and the template renders a non-Arabic body as one plain paragraph (pack: 'one

, no line breaks'). The order — history first, 'now a museum' two thirds down — is the source's. The Urdu already opens a sentence of its own on the museum; it may not reorder the page or break the paragraph. Harm: on a phone he lost his place twice.

The heading is the interface string trails.partOf (b0-ui), and 'Trails' reads as roads in the English too (logged there as a source defect; b1 observation 3). On the built page the routes are listed under it; his page shows a mark because no trail has an Urdu title yet. New from this reader for the interface batch: «راستہ» already stands for the breadcrumb («صفحے کا راستہ») and, in this batch, for the walkway of muhairis («چہل قدمی کا راستہ»).

CONFIRMED from the pack: access is told three ways in both languages. The row labelled 'Hours' holds a status and no hours ('Open for exterior visits', «متاح للزيارة الخارجية»); the next row says 'Free entry'; the body ends 'The site is undergoing restoration work, and some parts may be closed'. No reader can tell from the page whether the castle is entered, or at what hours one may come. The one part that was the Urdu's is answered by item N25: the row no longer ends on 'is open' (see the change). Not taken: his «صرف» — 'only' is an inference neither source states. What he made of the card: 'Three lines pull three ways … I cannot tell whether my family can go inside.'

Both sources name the page for the castle and write its body about the port: who built the castle, when, and what it looks like are in neither language, on a site whose other fort pages give all three.

'On the Arabian Gulf coast east of Al-Ahsa' is all either source gives, in the body and again in the area line: no distance, no drive, Al-Ahsa treated as a point (logged by b1 on the port's own page and by the Russian line). The summary names no place in either language. For open item P5 it is evidence: he read «خلیج کے ساحل پر» twice and did not ask which gulf.

'The emirate building' / «مبنى الإمارة» is all the sources say, and the Russian and German lines say no more; what the building was is not explained. The second half of the remark is the Urdu's and has no remedy inside the fence: «امارت» and «عمارت» side by side looked to him like a misprint (the proofreader had flagged the pair), and the one recorded alternative, «امارت کا دفتر», states a use the source does not state. Kept, and charged under nativeness and fit.
The opening in his words: «اسی بندرگاہ پر». Whose borders, between whom: 'demarcating borders' is all either source says, and nothing is supplied.
Applied for the clash he heard, not with his wording: «رونق» would say 'bustle' where both sources say 'role'. The noun stays and takes a verb it is attested with («کا کردار کم ہو گیا»).

The three are three places where both sources say 'witness' or 'attest' («شاهدة», «تشهد», «شاهداً»), in the summary and twice in the body; cutting or varying one would trade the content of its field for register (ruling P24). He calls the last 'a fine sentence on its own'. The repetition is logged with the source observations.

'The first seaport on Saudi Arabia's eastern coast' is the owner's ruled wording (build check C34), with no date and no sense of 'first' in either language — b1's reader stopped at the same two points on the port's own page — and 'seaport' is the source's own («ميناء بحري»). The claim stands in an apposition without a tense in both sources; the Urdu's «ہے» is the plain copula of a claim of rank, and a past tense would say that the port no longer holds it.
His wording, whole.

'They were restored in the late 1990s. The site is undergoing restoration work, and some parts may be closed' — two restorations in neighbouring sentences with nothing between them, in both languages (logged since stage 2). The second is a statement of status, kept at the source's strength: the Urdu adds no word of time to part the two, since that would fill a gap the source leaves. On record as a one-line option for the owner: «ان دنوں اس مقام پر مرمت کا کام جاری ہے».

«مسجد الجبری» is the mosque's reference title (verified entry), with the article that keeps the builder and the mosque on one word (item N27). The first glance at «جبری» is the reason the dynasty is «بنو جبر» and not an adjective (item N28), and he says the summary 'settles it as a name'.

The source says it twice, in both languages: 'Entry: A working mosque, no entry fee' («مسجد عامل، بلا رسوم دخول») and 'Fees: Free entry' («مجاني») (pack, reviewed divergences). Both rows are translated as they stand; a card row is not dropped or merged in a translation. That talk of a fee reads strangely to a Muslim reader of a mosque page is logged for the owner.

The page has no hours row in any language and the template still shows its notice about hours. When a visitor who is not coming to pray may enter, and anything about women, is in no source: the owner's question on working mosques outside prayer times is open, and the Urdu states no visiting time. Harm: someone who would come both to pray and to look cannot tell whether the mosque is open between prayers.

The fixed visiting row as b1's judge ruled it on this observation and its own reader's: a semicolon, then two requests; byte for byte b1's. The label «زیارت» stays: item N17, ruled for every mosque page — the two readers part on the weight of the word, this one on an ordinary working mosque, b1's on Jawatha, and neither offers another label; his remark is recorded with that item. Not taken from his wording: «مسجد کے آداب» for the source's 'sanctity of the place'. That the row seems written for someone who has never been inside a mosque is the owner-fixed wording itself.

The phrase says the source's 'intersecting vaults' («تقاطع أقبيته») in plain words: roofs, vaulted, crossing one another. He offers no wording, Urdu has no everyday noun for a vault, and every plainer phrase weighed since stage 1 drops either the vaulting or the crossing, a distinction both sources make. Kept, and charged under nativeness: he read it twice and could not picture it.

«بیلن نما» is the school-geometry word for the source's 'cylindrical' («أسطوانية»); his «گول» says 'round', which is another word of these pages (the round tower of muhairis) and less than the source says of the minaret's shape: a trade of content for register (ruling P24). He understood it. One-line option for the owner: «اس کا مینار گول ہے».
Both points: «یوں» is gone, and «درس و تدریس» is his. One departure from his wording: «اور علم» stays beside it, because 'scholarship' is in both sources and his phrase alone would drop it.

His second clause, without «ہی»: the materials now follow the verb. His «آخری بار اس کی مرمت» is not needed once the stack is undone. «منصوبے کے تحت» and «تعمیراتی مواد» stay: the programme is the source's, and the bare noun for materials is first read in Urdu as 'content' (stage 4).
His wording: «پرانے ہفوف».
His wording: «یہ آج بھی ایک آباد مسجد ہے۔». His 'exactly right' confirms b1's item N26.

'Around 850 AH / 1446 CE' is the sources' own pair («نحو عام 850هـ/1446م»): an approximate Hijri year beside an exact-looking Gregorian one. Nothing is computed or rounded (b1's item N12); whether the Gregorian year is approximate too is not said.

Item N14: after this round the batch has one form for one Arabic generic — «قصر محیرس», «قصر خزام», and «قصر ابراہیم» in passing — and «قلعہ العقیر» for the one whose Arabic name says «قلعة». The 'Palace' of the two English titles beside 'Qasr Ibrahim' is the source's split and is logged.

Applied on the three fort pages (changes m-open, k-verb, u-verb): where a building is, is said with «واقع ہے», as on the mosque page. «… محلہ الکوت میں ہے» of the house stays: plain Urdu, and not the verb he faults. Recorded for b1, whose sahood has the twin opening.

The sources differ: muhairis was 'built … by order of Saud bin Abdulaziz' («شُيّد … بأمر»), khuzam 'built … by Imam Saud bin Abdulaziz' («بناها الإمام»). The causative on one page and the plain verb on the other say what each page says of the same man.

Not settled in the text: logged as item N30 of this file with both candidate forms. The rows differ because the sources' area lines differ ('Al-Koot district — central Hofuf' on baiah, 'Al-Koot district — Hofuf' on jabri-mosque; only muhairis names Al-Ahsa) and because ruling P20 puts a larger place first only where the source names one as a bare name. Six area lines of the two attraction batches follow the source's order for want of such a name; a rule for them binds b1 and every later page and is not made here on one minor remark.

Three rulings, none reopened. The spacing: item N27 (b1 round 1), names built on «عبد» in two words, on the reference titles of the very persons — a reader's preference for the joined spelling does not overrule a form taken from a reference title; his remark is recorded as an option for the owner (joined: «عبدالعزیز», «عبدالرحمن», «عبداللطیف», the spelling of the reader's paper). The article: ruling P1, every place name as the Arabic writes it except the closed list of settled Urdu forms, of which «ہفوف» is one. The month: the verified entry «جمادی الاول» (the reference title; the other spelling needs a letter the letterform rule does not admit, or a superscript sign); he says both are seen.

The sources put the same kind of news in a different place on each page: on khuzam the closure is a card row labelled 'Current status' and absent from the body; on uqair-castle the works are the last sentence of the body, there is no status row, and the status sits under 'Hours'. Each page follows its own source.

source_defects.where: khuzam: body and summary against practical[0] (observation 17, serious; also 65)
source_defects.defect: The closure stands in one card row only. The body says the fort was 'restored and opened to visitors in 2017' and stops there; the summary, which is the page's search description and its index card, says nothing of a closure; the card says 'currently closed for restoration and heritage development' and gives no date of reopening and no word on whether the outside can be seen meanwhile. Both languages agree with each other, and the owner confirmed on 2026-10-12 that the fort is closed and that both statements stand as they are.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Both statements are carried at their source's strength with no word between them: no 'but', no 'again', no 'for now'. HARM, the greatest on these five pages: a reader of the search result, the index card or the body alone takes the fort for open — 'Had I stopped at the paragraph, I would have gone' — and the one who reaches the card cannot plan.

source_defects.where: uqair-castle: practical[0], practical[1] and the last body sentence (observation 39, serious; also 40, 41, 65)
source_defects.defect: Access is told three ways, in both languages: a row labelled 'Hours' that holds a status and no hours ('Open for exterior visits'), a row that says 'Free entry', and a body that ends 'The site is undergoing restoration work, and some parts may be closed' straight after 'They were restored in the late 1990s'. The page is named for the castle and says nothing of the castle itself — builder, date, shape — and gives no distance from any town.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The status row now follows the Arabic's construction («باہر سے دیکھا جا سکتا ہے») so that the Urdu does not add an 'open' of its own; no 'only' and no hours are supplied; the other two statements stand as they are. HARM: 'Three lines pull three ways … I cannot tell whether my family can go inside', nor at what hours, nor how far it is.

source_defects.where: muhairis: practical[0], practical[1] and the end of the body (observation 14, serious; also 9)
source_defects.defect: The only hours on the page are those of 'the garden and walkway'; 'Free entry' does not say to what; the body calls the same green space a park and the card a garden; and nothing says whether the fort itself, which the body leaves 'out of use', can be entered. The page never says what Al-Mubarraz is, and places the fort 'on the edge of' it in one line and 'north of' it in two.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The cell names what the hours belong to before the hours, as both sources do; two source nouns stay two Urdu words; nothing is supplied. HARM: 'I would drive the family there not knowing whether we will see a fort from inside or take an evening walk beside a wall.'

source_defects.defect: The source has no hours for the mosque and nothing on when a visitor who is not coming to pray may enter, or on women (the owner's question on working mosques is open); it says that nothing is charged in two rows and two wordings ('Entry: a working mosque, no entry fee', 'Fees: free entry'), and its row labelled 'Entry' answers with 'a working mosque'. The template then shows its notice about hours and fees under a card that has no hours.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Both rows are translated as they stand and no visiting time is stated or implied. HARM: a reader who would come both to pray and to look cannot tell whether the mosque is open between prayers, and the talk of a fee reads strangely to a Muslim reader.

source_defects.where: muhairis and khuzam, with baiah: the builder (observations 11, 12, 62)
source_defects.defect: One ruler under two treatments — 'Saud bin Abdulaziz (later Imam)', by whose order the first fort was built, and 'Imam Saud bin Abdulaziz, third imam of the First Saudi State', who built the second — and neither page says that 'Imam' is here a ruler's title. No page separates him from the King Abdulaziz of 1913, whose name his father shares.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Each page says what its source says («جو بعد میں امام بنے»; the causative on one page, the plain verb on the other). HARM: a reader of muhairis alone takes the builder for a man who later became a prayer leader, and the year 1794 beside a name he knows from recent kings made him reread it.

source_defects.where: khuzam: the name, the measure, the placing, the status wording (observations 18, 19, 22, 24)
source_defects.defect: The name is said to come from 'zimam' with no word on how; the wall is 'roughly 70 by 80 metres' with neither figure called the length, beside a sister page that gives its measure in words; the fort is on Hofuf's 'western edge', 'in western Hofuf' and 'west of Hofuf'; 'heritage development' is not explained, and the status says 'at present' twice (label and value).
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The source's explanation of the name is kept as it is — the reader suspected a typing slip; the measure names neither length nor breadth; the placing is as open as the Arabic's; the status keeps both of its words for 'now'.

source_defects.defect: title_en says 'Palace' of two buildings that both languages then call forts, beside 'Qasr Ibrahim' on a sister page; neither page has a sentence that bridges the name and the building; 'Khuzam Palace' shares its name with a palace in Jeddah.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: One Urdu form after this round, «قصر X» (item N14). A reader for whom «قصر» is a palace still passes from the name to «قلعہ» with nothing between.

source_defects.where: baiah: the body as a whole and its details (observations 26, 29, 31, 32, 35, 37; 33 and 34 in part)
source_defects.defect: The English body is one paragraph of 1331 characters where the Arabic has five, and says 'now a museum' only after all the history; 'known as Bayt Al-Mulla' does not say which name is in use; '(1853–1921)' is unlabelled and Gregorian only on a page that leads with Hijri years; two men named Abdulrahman stand 65 years apart with nothing said; 'the Saudi state' and 'the modern Saudi state' in sentences that repeat each other; 'historical and political landmarks'; 'explanatory photographs'; whose clothing is on show; a body named with a 'Saudi' the Arabic does not have.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: One word of form is repaired under ruling P23 («… کے نام سے بھی معروف ہے»; the literal wording is on record). Everything else is as the source has it; on a phone the reader lost his place twice.

source_defects.defect: 'The first seaport' with no date and no sense of 'first', in an apposition without a tense, and a 'seaport' that says the sea twice; 'demarcating borders' without saying whose; 'the emirate building' unexplained; the witness image three times on a short page; two restorations in neighbouring sentences with nothing between them.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The owner-ruled claim keeps its wording and its present tense; no word of time is put between the two restorations (the option is on record); «امارت کی عمارت» stays word for word and looked to the reader like a misprint.

source_defects.defect: The English summary turns the Arabic's ninth Hijri century into 'the fifteenth century' and names no calendar; 'around 850 AH / 1446 CE' sets an approximate year beside an exact-looking one; the English drops the issuing of fatwas; 'original materials' does not say whether the very materials or the same kind; 'intersecting vaults' and 'a cylindrical minaret' are an architect's words on a visitor's page.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The century follows the English with its calendar word, nothing computed (the Arabic's form is on record); the pair of years is not rounded; the two architectural phrases are said in plain words, and the reader could not picture the first and smiled at the second.

source_defects.where: the template on these five pages (observations 1, 5, 20, 38; 2, 3, 4 and the card heading of 6 are interface wordings)
source_defects.defect: The notice under the card sends the visitor to 'the management of this place' on five pages that have no operator link, and appears under cards with no hours; the World Heritage badge prints a bare component number; a photo's accessible name is the title and a number; 'Trails' reads as roads.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: None on this batch's fields: interface strings and template behaviour of b0-ui, recorded for its next round.

source_defects.defect: 'Watch' three times in six sentences (the summary's 'watch-and-guard fort', the body's, and 'a lookout post'); 'festival seasons' neither named nor dated; one of the Arabic's three building materials dropped by the English.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The repetition stays; no festival and no date is supplied; the English's two materials.

source_defects.where: across pages: area lines and where a closure is told (observations 63, 65)
source_defects.defect: The same district is 'Al-Koot district — central Hofuf' on one page and 'Al-Koot district — Hofuf' on another, and only one of five area lines names Al-Ahsa; news of a closure or of works is a card row on one page and the last body sentence on another.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Each page follows its source; the order of an area line without a larger bare place is left open (item N30).

calibration.question: The gloss for a name whose Arabic generic is opaque or a false friend in Urdu, in running text: its form and where it is owed (raised by this batch's stage 4 with what b2's pages add).
candidates: A — the named gloss «(یعنی … کا …)» on every such name, passing mentions included
B — the same form, owed only on the page whose own name it is; a name met in passing stands bare
C — on a passing mention the Urdu generic in apposition after «نامی», no bracket
calibration.evidence: Ruled in b1 round 1 on both readers; binding here and applied, not reopened. What this batch's reader adds. FORM AND SCOPE: «بیت البیعہ (یعنی بیعت کا گھر)», the page's own name, 'clears it at once' (observation 25) — he had first taken «البیعہ» in the title from the word for a sale; the souq's bracket in passing 'tells me سوق is بازار, which I could guess, but not what القیصریہ is', and was 'the second (یعنی …) bracket in two sentences' (observation 30). The bare «قصر ابراہیم», in passing on two pages, drew no remark on the missing gloss; what he noticed is the split of name forms (observation 60), which item N14 ends. A FOURTH GENERIC, «بیت»: an Urdu dictionary word for a house whose first sense is a verse (stage 4); as a page title it takes the bracket form because the English source itself glosses the name.
calibration.ruling_or_recommendation: As b1 round 1 ruled it (its five points), adopted. On b2's pages: (1) «بیت البیعہ (یعنی بیعت کا گھر)» stays, once, at the first mention in its own body (point 4: a page title that is an Arabic phrase with a meaning takes this form, not the quotation marks of ruling P3b); «بیت الملا» beside it is bare. (2) The souq in passing on baiah is «سوق القیصریہ نامی بازار», as on b1's ameeriah; «قصر ابراہیم» in passing on baiah and jabri-mosque is bare. (3) The two «(عربی میں …)» brackets are gone with item N14. RIDER, a case the ruling did not foresee, ruled narrowly here: where the name that takes «نامی» and its Urdu generic stands in a list with another name, it goes FIRST («سوق القیصریہ نامی بازار اور قصر ابراہیم»), because after two names joined by «اور» the words «نامی بازار» can be read of both.
calibration.binds: baiah body (two places); the rider binds any later sentence that lists such a name with another; recorded for b1's next round (its one such sentence, on ameeriah, has no second name).
calibration.guard: b1's, as written under this id in b1/stages/07-judge.round1.json; not repeated here, so that one file owns each machine-read clause. For the proofreader, not machine-read: a name followed by «نامی» and its generic is not the second member of a list of names.

calibration.question: Large numbers and their scale; and a figure below one lakh.
candidates: A — «1,600»: digits and separator as the English writes them (in the text)
B — «1600», as the Arabic writes it
calibration.evidence: The scale was ruled in b0-ui and a line on figures below one lakh was added in b1 round 1; the ruling's text is repeated below word for word because the tools read it. What this batch adds: jabri-mosque body, 'around 1,600 worshippers' (EN) / «لنحو 1600 مصلٍّ» (AR), written «تقریباً 1,600 نمازیوں کی گنجائش ہے» in the reference's own frame for a mosque's capacity («نمازیوں کی گنجائش» 127 pages). The reader read the sentence without a remark.
calibration.ruling_or_recommendation: B. Counts in /ur/ text are written in the Urdu scale, in digits with the scale word: million = 10 «لاکھ», ten million = 1 «کروڑ», a thousand million = 1 «ارب»; thousands as the source («16,000»); a decimal is kept where the conversion leaves one («1.5 لاکھ»). 'More than' is «سے زیادہ» in a sentence. «ملین» and «بلین» are not written. The big figure of the home page takes the compact form, «25 لاکھ+», which is the source's own form; the lead says «25 لاکھ سے زیادہ». Not exercised and not ruled: a sum of money in a foreign currency. Added in b1 round 1: a figure below one lakh is written in digits, grouped as the English source groups it («10,000», «1,600»); the Urdu scale begins at one lakh.
calibration.guard: Stage checker (taught after round 1; it reads this entry): where the English or Arabic carries a figure followed by million / M / «مليون», the Urdu carries the same value written with the scale words above — ten times the figure followed by «لاکھ», or a tenth of it followed by «کروڑ» from ten million up; a wrong conversion, a bare converted figure or an unconverted one is a finding. The clauses of the ruling ('million = 10 …', 'ten million = 1 …', 'a thousand million = 1 …', '… and … are not written') are what the tools parse and are to be kept word for word when the ruling is entered in the termbase. Build check on /ur/: «ملین» and «بلین» as whole words do not occur.

(1) khuzam: the summary has «قلعہ», but the first body sentence only places the fort («قصر خزام ہفوف کے مغرب میں … واقع ہے۔»), as it has since stage 1; the common noun comes in the sentence straight after it («یہ قلعہ 1220 ہجری … تعمیر کیا»). NARROW RULING on the case the ruling's wording did not foresee ('in its summary and in its first body sentence'): the point is met when the common noun stands in the summary and in the first OR the second sentence of the body, before any other fact about the building — as it does on both pages; neither body is rewritten to move it. The cost b1's judge stated holds on both pages and is what the next blind reader is asked to show: a reader for whom «قصر» is a palace meets «قلعہ» in the next line with nothing between.
